changes.after: Share a declaration through a header and guard against repeated inclusion.

before: A header is text included into a translation unit (one source file after preprocessing its includes). A declaration tells the compiler about a name and its type. A class definition such as struct Score may also live in a header when the language’s definition rules are respected.

Save this as score.hpp beside main.cpp:
```cpp
#ifndef SCORE_HPP
#define SCORE_HPP
struct Score { int value; };
#endif
```
The first inclusion defines SCORE_HPP. On the second inclusion, #ifndef is false, so the guarded definition is skipped. These preprocessor directives are not runtime if statements.

The source below intentionally includes the header twice. Compile main.cpp with the header available to the compiler. Use standard include guards rather than relying on a particular compiler’s #pragma once extension for this example.
Expected output or behavior: 3. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Add a second header that also includes score.hpp and explain why the guarded definition remains usable. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: A header is a file of code that another source file can include. A declaration introduces a name and its type. Here score.hpp defines the Score type so main.cpp can use it.
#include brings a header's text into the source before compilation. One source file with its included text forms a translation unit: the code the compiler processes together.

An include guard prevents the same header contents from being included twice in that unit. #ifndef checks whether SCORE_HPP is undefined. #define marks it as defined, so the second inclusion skips the guarded text.
The program prints 3. The guard lets Score be defined once even though main.cpp includes the header twice.
The # directives are handled before the program runs. Including a header twice does not run it twice. Without the guard, this unit would contain two definitions of Score, which is an error.

before.question: Remove the guard lines from score.hpp but keep both includes. What happens in this translation unit?
choices: Compilation rejects the repeated Score definition.
It prints 6 because the header is run twice.
The linker automatically merges both class definitions.
before.explanation: Both include directives now paste the same struct definition into one translation unit. That is a redefinition, not a second execution.

after.question: Remove the guard lines from score.hpp but keep both includes. What happens?
choices: The compiler rejects the repeated Score definition in the same translation unit.
The program prints 6 because the header runs twice.
The linker automatically combines the repeated definitions.
after.explanation: Both includes bring in the same struct definition. The error is a repeated definition, not repeated execution.
